title: From physics to products
summary: The Work Passport begins in August 2017, after the PhD chapter. A transition into industry led to the Physics Project Manager role at Hawkes Learning (November 2017–January 2018), coordinating physics courseware development. August is the archive boundary, not a claimed employment start date.

title: Antennas, arrays & leadership
summary: Joined Northrop Grumman in Baltimore in January 2018. Early assignments included algorithm development for an internal computational electromagnetics toolkit and installed-performance analysis for SEWIP. RAPTR followed as a scalable radar product-line offering aimed at Army Future Vertical Lift and drone radar applications; additive-manufactured antenna development primarily supported the company's proposed Navy Future X-Band Radar (FXR) offering. Later responsibilities included leadership of a 16-person engineering group.

title: Systems at mission scale
summary: My move to Boulder in September 2021 was an advancement from Manager 2 to Manager 3, and an adjustment from a large site and small local team to a smaller home site and a much larger geographically distributed systems engineering organization. I led an OPIR ground-processing section of roughly 50 engineers across four managers, hired and developed people, and spent time connecting with teams and leadership at Azusa, Space Park and Dayton. Dayton-based colleagues worked with NASIC at Wright-Patterson AFB. Alongside management, I learned the OPIR mission space, worked on major capture pursuits and color-team reviews, and participated in the Space Sector intellectual-property community. RGS-A was my first major space-to-ground communications assignment, from capture RF technical volume to SEIT leadership and two Guam visits. I transitioned from functional management into a continuous Senior Staff technical-leadership role in November 2025, with the Chief Engineer title following in April 2026. The website treats this as one role. Boulder remained my Northrop Grumman career base throughout. In the smaller Boulder environment, I learned to slow down, listen more and practice patience. My subsequent technical assignments have reinforced how much I enjoy serving as a hands-on technical authority while still taking satisfaction in helping other engineers grow.
